title: Scope Deposit Ledger
user: A solo trade or professional-services operator who takes a deposit or retainer and needs to show exactly which agreed scope it is held against and when it becomes billable.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN: ‘How do you do invoicing?’ is a direct current request for practical invoicing workflow.
A self-hosted Invoice Ninja user says professional-services and trades clients prepay deposits/retainers and requests a deposit invoice whose payment can be applied correctly later.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 askers, one broad and one explicit trade/professional-services workflow. Deposit misallocation directly causes invoice disputes and cash-reporting errors.
current_workaround: Create a normal invoice, keep a note or spreadsheet of the deposit, then manually apply a credit when the final invoice is sent.
incumbents_and_gap: Invoice Ninja, QuickBooks, Xero, and Jobber can invoice and record payments, but their full accounting/job suites make a scope-level deposit trail hard to hand to a client without adopting the whole system.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA for one operator: create a scope, record a deposit, allocate it across milestones, and export a client-readable PDF/CSV balance trail. Non-goals: payment processing, general ledger, tax filing, or a CRM.
success_measure: In a 30-day pilot, 10 of 12 deposited jobs have a generated allocation trail and no pilot operator needs a separate spreadsheet to answer ‘what did this deposit cover?’
monetization: one-time — the core value is a durable local record for occasional or seasonal jobs, not another monthly finance suite.
constraints: All job and client data stays on-device by default; exports must make tax jurisdiction assumptions explicit; never present balances as accounting advice.
why_distinct: It is a narrow deposit-to-scope evidence ledger, not an invoice generator or payments clone.

title: Billable Split
user: A contractor buying materials for several jobs at once who must split one supplier receipt into billable, non-billable, and reimbursable job costs without losing the source record.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A founder asks how people manage bank reconciliations and invoice processing and whether the work still has substantial manual data entry.
A contractor billing time-and-materials requests independent categories, amounts, and billable flags for multiple lines on one vendor invoice.

recurrence: Independent 2025 and 2026 requests identify receipt/invoice entry as manual; the contractor report gives the concrete multi-job failure mode.
current_workaround: Photograph the receipt, duplicate it in a spreadsheet or accounting package, and later reconstruct the split from memory.
incumbents_and_gap: QuickBooks, Xero, Dext, and Invoice Ninja capture expenses, but they center accounting records or OCR and do not make a fast, local, line-by-line job allocation slip the primary object.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA that stores a receipt image, creates manual line items, allocates each line across jobs with billable flags, and exports per-job CSV/PDF evidence. Non-goals: OCR promises, bank feeds, bookkeeping automation, or tax returns.
success_measure: At least 75% of pilot receipts are allocated within 24 hours, and each pilot can export a complete source-to-job cost packet at month end.
monetization: one-time — a private, offline utility is preferable for small operators handling intermittent material purchases.
constraints: Receipt images can contain payment and tax information; encrypt local backups and allow permanent deletion; allocation export must retain immutable source-image hashes.
why_distinct: The product solves the allocation decision after capture; it is neither a receipt scanner nor a full expense-accounting clone.

title: Early Pay Terms
user: A tiny B2B supplier who offers an early-payment discount and needs each invoice to show the exact discounted amount, deadline, and remaining payable amount without ambiguous manual maths.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN poster says chasing overdue B2B invoices is manual at both work and a family business; the thread has 30 comments.
An Invoice Ninja feature request with 11 comments calls native early-payment discount/‘Skonto’ handling common in Germany, Switzerland, and Austria.

recurrence: Two 2026 reports, including a 30-comment overdue-payment thread and a multi-comment regional-payment-terms request. Errors affect both collection speed and the amount due.
current_workaround: Write discount wording manually on PDFs, calculate the amount in a calculator, and remember to change the balance after a payment arrives.
incumbents_and_gap: QuickBooks, Xero, Invoice Ninja, and ERPs handle invoices, but localized early-pay terms often require configuration or an accounting workflow too large for a small supplier.
smallest_useful_product: A local terms calculator and invoice attachment generator: choose discount basis, tax treatment, dates, and currency rounding; emit a clear payment card and paid-on-time receipt. Non-goals: issuing invoices, collecting payment, accounting entries, or legal/tax advice.
success_measure: For 50 pilot invoices, the tool’s displayed amount equals the operator’s independently checked amount in 100% of cases and users report fewer payment clarification emails.
monetization: one-time — calculation correctness and document reuse are enduring, low-frequency utility value.
constraints: Regional VAT and discount rules vary; require the user to select and verify terms, version calculations, and clearly disclaim legal/accounting advice.
why_distinct: It makes one payment term legible and auditable rather than competing as a general invoicing platform.

title: Quote to Cash Trail
user: A freelancer or micro-business owner who needs to answer a client question by tracing one job from quote through approval, invoice, payment, and delivery evidence.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN asks freelancers which invoicing features matter and what current tools get wrong or overcomplicate.
An ERPNext user requests a visual relationship map because tracing a transaction from quotation to payment is not currently straightforward.

recurrence: The 2025 freelancer request and a 2026 ERP feature request independently identify an overcomplicated invoicing workflow and missing document traceability.
current_workaround: Search email, quotes, PDFs, bank exports, and a CRM/accounting suite separately; send screenshots when a client asks for status.
incumbents_and_gap: ERPNext, Odoo, QuickBooks, and CRMs hold many of these documents, but their relationship views are broad ERP navigation rather than a shareable single-job evidence trail.
smallest_useful_product: Local-first job dossier accepting drag-dropped PDFs/CSVs and manual links, showing a linear quote→approval→invoice→payment→handoff trail and exporting one static client packet. Non-goals: invoice creation, payment rails, document e-signature, or CRM pipelines.
success_measure: In a pilot, users assemble a complete status packet for 80% of sampled jobs in under three minutes without searching email.
monetization: one-time — the product is a portable evidence binder, suited to local archival rather than a hosted suite.
constraints: Documents may include PII and payment references; local encryption and explicit export controls are required; users remain responsible for retention requirements.
why_distinct: It is a read-only, client-readable relationship trail across existing tools, not another ERP or quoting system.

title: Subcontract Client Brief
user: A subcontractor serving an agency, builder, or property manager who needs to keep the contracting client, end customer, site contacts, scope, and handoff obligations unambiguously separated.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A solo carpenter says $150+/month field-service software was bloated and too expensive for a one-person operation, motivating a narrower tool.
A self-hosted Invoice Ninja user requests an end-client (‘sub-client’) relationship spanning clients, projects, tasks, and invoices for subcontracted work.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 field-service/subcontracting reports point to a mismatch between small operators’ workflows and large service-suite data models.
current_workaround: Duplicate the end customer in a CRM, put names in free-text notes, and rely on email threads to remember who may approve work or receive files.
incumbents_and_gap: Jobber, ServiceTitan, Invoice Ninja, and CRMs support customers and jobs, but a lightweight, portable contracting-client versus end-client handoff brief is not their primary artifact.
smallest_useful_product: Encrypted offline PWA with a two-party job card: contracting client, end client/site, authorized contacts, scope, access notes, deliverables, and a sign-off export. Non-goals: dispatch, invoices, payment collection, or full CRM.
success_measure: A pilot subcontractor can produce an accurate handoff brief for 90% of active jobs without copying contacts from email, and records zero wrong-recipient handoffs over 30 days.
monetization: one-time — small subcontractors need a private job artifact, not per-seat field-service subscription pricing.
constraints: Store personally identifiable contact and site-access information locally; support device lock/export redaction; do not imply legal authorization or contract management.
why_distinct: Its core model is the often-lost relationship between payer and end recipient, rather than generic customer management.

title: Settlement Match
user: A one-store ecommerce or service business owner who needs to explain why a processor payout differs from that day’s orders and invoices without linking a bank account to another SaaS.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A small ecommerce reconciliation prototype asks how businesses match Shopify, payment-provider, and accounting numbers and explain mismatches.
An Invoice Ninja user reports that a Stripe deposit bundles prior-day payments and can only be matched to one transaction after CSV import.

recurrence: Two independent reports in 2025–26 describe the same settlement-versus-sales mismatch; this is a month-end blocker rather than an optional dashboard feature.
current_workaround: Download processor and order CSVs, use spreadsheet formulas, and attach a note to one deposit or ask a bookkeeper to reconstruct it.
incumbents_and_gap: A2X, Link My Books, QuickBooks, Xero, and Invoice Ninja offer reconciliation paths, but are subscription suites, integrations, or single-transaction matchers rather than a local explainable payout bundle tool.
smallest_useful_product: Local CSV matcher for one processor payout and one sales/invoice export: reconcile gross sales, fees, refunds, timing shifts, and produce a signed-off exception report. Non-goals: bank connectivity, automatic posting, tax reporting, or multi-store analytics.
success_measure: Pilot users explain at least 95% of imported payout variance and reduce manual reconciliation time for one payout by 50% against their existing spreadsheet process.
monetization: one-time — users can bring their own CSV exports and retain sensitive financial data locally.
constraints: CSV data includes customer and financial data; process entirely in-browser, offer deletion, and require mapping confirmation; no accounting certification claims.
why_distinct: It explains one payout bundle deterministically instead of being another accounting system or payments integration.

title: Actuals Job Sequencer
user: A solo or two-person trade business scheduling dependent job steps who needs the next promised dates to move when the prior step actually finishes late.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN asks whether anyone has deployed tools in a trade or field-service business and what worked, showing active demand for workable operational tooling.
An ERPNext user explains that dependent task timelines stay fixed even when real-world work is delayed and asks for finish-to-start auto-scheduling from actuals.

recurrence: Two 2026 sources in trade/field-service and project operations point to schedule drift after real work departs from a baseline plan.
current_workaround: Maintain a whiteboard or spreadsheet, change every downstream date manually, then text clients if someone notices the collision.
incumbents_and_gap: Jobber, ServiceTitan, ERPNext, and Microsoft Project support scheduling, but carry dispatch/ERP complexity; tiny crews need a few job dependencies and a revised promise date, offline.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA for up to five active jobs: ordered steps, actual finish date, non-working days, dependency shifts, and a concise ‘dates changed’ client message. Non-goals: route optimization, staff payroll, GPS tracking, or a general Gantt suite.
success_measure: At least 80% of downstream dates update correctly in a seeded test set, and pilots send client updates within one business day of a blocked step.
monetization: one-time — it targets very small crews priced out of recurring field-service suites.
constraints: No location tracking; export dates with timezone and holiday settings; make clear that forecast dates are user-entered estimates.
why_distinct: It recomputes only the consequences of actual job progress; it is not a dispatch platform or generic project manager.

title: Booking Side Notes
user: A small appointment business that needs to keep operational notes—call back, access detail, follow-up, supplier delay—visible beside a booking without falsely blocking another appointment slot.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN asks how small businesses handle appointment reminders and whether they still rely on simple/manual setups rather than full scheduling platforms.
An Easy!Appointments user asks for calendar notes that record daily operational information but do not affect availability or block bookings.

recurrence: Two 2026 sources distinguish real small-business calendar work from full booking logic; notes that consume capacity create missed opportunities.
current_workaround: Put notes in a separate notebook, a private calendar, or fake appointments that accidentally make time unavailable.
incumbents_and_gap: Calendly, Google Calendar, Cal.com, and Easy!Appointments handle bookings; their events often conflate visible operational context with capacity-blocking time.
smallest_useful_product: Local companion PWA that imports a day’s ICS events and attaches nonblocking, time-anchored notes, checkboxes, and reminder status; print or export a daily brief. Non-goals: public booking pages, SMS delivery, calendar hosting, or CRM.
success_measure: In a four-week pilot, users record 90% of operational notes in the companion and no note creates an accidental unavailable booking slot.
monetization: one-time — it complements existing calendars rather than taking over recurring booking infrastructure.
constraints: ICS files and notes can contain client PII; default to local storage, minimize event fields, and avoid background sync without opt-in.
why_distinct: It explicitly separates operational context from availability, a smaller problem than appointment scheduling itself.

title: Service Notification Router
user: A micro-clinic, studio, or multi-service office where a booking must alert the right service coordinator without giving every staff member every booking notification.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A small-scale seller asks about Calendly-to-WhatsApp integration on the free plan, highlighting the cost and integration friction around booking notifications.
An Easy!Appointments user requests service-specific notifications so secretaries for different providers receive only the appointments they cover.

recurrence: Two August 2026 requests independently focus on getting booking notifications to the right channel/person without paying for or building a large automation stack.
current_workaround: Forward all booking email to a shared inbox or WhatsApp group, manually forward it, or use an expensive scheduler tier/automation service.
incumbents_and_gap: Calendly, Cal.com, Zapier, Make, and Easy!Appointments have notifications and integrations, but simple service-to-recipient routing is buried in plan tiers or generalized automation.
smallest_useful_product: Self-hosted rules endpoint: receive a normalized booking email/webhook, map service/provider to a recipient, add a minimal acknowledgment link, and purge payloads after a configured interval. Non-goals: booking pages, WhatsApp scraping, marketing messages, or workforce management.
success_measure: In a 30-day pilot, 95% of booking notices reach the configured responsible recipient and shared-group notification volume falls by at least 60%.
monetization: one-time — a self-hosted operational router avoids per-task automation pricing and keeps appointment data under the business’s control.
constraints: Obtain consent for email/SMS channels; verify webhook signatures; encrypt retained data; comply with provider messaging policies and do not automate unsolicited outreach.
why_distinct: It is a narrow responsibility router for already-created bookings, not a scheduler or generic automation canvas.

title: Shared Capacity Slots
user: A two-to-five-person service business with different services, staff, rooms, or equipment who needs to expose real capacity without one person’s calendar falsely blocking another service.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Ask HN asks what people find most annoying about scheduling meetings and what could be made easier; the thread has four responses.
A Cal.com request with 14 comments says one calendar cannot allow overlapping event types even when different team members deliver different services.

recurrence: A 2026 open scheduling question and a 14-comment 2025 calendar issue identify availability rules, not page design, as the hard recurring problem.
current_workaround: Create separate calendars or event types, overblock time, accept bookings manually, or buy a larger scheduling product.
incumbents_and_gap: Calendly, Cal.com, Acuity, and SimplyBook.me support teams, but their resource models can be complex or subscription-gated for a tiny mixed-service shop.
smallest_useful_product: Offline capacity simulator: define people/resources/service requirements, import busy ICS blocks, calculate offerable slots, and export an availability table/ICS feed. Non-goals: public booking UI, payments, staff surveillance, or enterprise resource planning.
success_measure: For a representative four-week schedule, its proposed slots produce zero resource conflicts and recover at least 10% more valid slots than a single shared calendar.
monetization: one-time — a capacity planning layer can sit beside existing calendars without a per-user booking subscription.
constraints: ICS import must stay local by default; timezone/DST behavior needs exhaustive tests; output is advisory and must not silently create bookings.
why_distinct: It calculates a small service-capacity matrix and deliberately stops before becoming another appointment-booking SaaS.

title: Backfill Timecards
user: A freelancer who records a week of work after the fact and needs to reconstruct, copy, and associate repeated time entries with the right client/project before invoicing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A freelancer asks how people track development time now that work includes prompting, reviewing, and waiting for AI agents rather than continuous active coding.
A Kimai user entering 30–50 time-sheet rows per week asks that selecting a unique project automatically fill its customer because small entry improvements accumulate.

recurrence: Independent July/August 2026 users describe time capture that is retrospective and high-volume, with AI-era work making conventional timers less representative.
current_workaround: Run a timer imperfectly, rely on calendar history and memory, then copy/paste entries in a spreadsheet or timesheet system at week end.
incumbents_and_gap: Toggl, Harvest, Clockify, Kimai, and Timely track time, but most optimize live timers or reporting rather than a quick, privacy-preserving retrospective reconstruction flow.
smallest_useful_product: Offline weekly board that imports calendar events, clones prior patterns, fills project→client mappings, records explainable work blocks, and exports invoice-ready CSV. Non-goals: employee monitoring, screenshots, automatic AI time inference, payroll, or invoicing.
success_measure: Pilot freelancers complete a 30-entry retrospective week in under 15 minutes and report that 90% of exported rows need no correction before invoicing.
monetization: one-time — freelancers should own sensitive work-history data and not pay a recurring fee for a weekly utility.
constraints: Calendar event text may be confidential; import locally, allow selective fields, and provide data export/deletion; never infer billable time automatically.
why_distinct: It supports honest retrospective reconstruction, not surveillance-style automatic time tracking or a full project suite.

title: Shelf Walk Stocktake
user: A single-location wholesaler, workshop, or retailer doing a physical stock count who needs a fast barcode-assisted walk in shelf order and a defensible variance file without deploying an ERP.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A family wholesale/distribution business asks whether others still run on a 1993 on-premise TUI; the discussion has 96 comments, showing durable small-business operational-system constraints.
An InvenTree feature request says a selector showing only the last segment of a shelf location is insufficient to distinguish stock locations.

recurrence: A 96-comment 2025 distribution-system discussion and a 2026 inventory-location request both show that physical stock work must survive legacy systems and unambiguous real-world locations.
current_workaround: Print a shelf list, count into paper or a spreadsheet, scan into a generic inventory app, then reconcile location ambiguities later.
incumbents_and_gap: InvenTree, Odoo, Zoho Inventory, Sortly, and spreadsheets manage stock, but small operators need an offline count pass ordered by a human shelf path—not a replacement warehouse system.
smallest_useful_product: Offline mobile PWA: import item/location CSV, show full shelf path, scan or search an item, record count/reason/photo note, and export only variances plus an audit CSV. Non-goals: POS, purchasing, valuation, multi-warehouse sync, or ERP integration.
success_measure: In a pilot count of 300 SKUs, 95% of scans are assigned to the intended full location and the variance file is ready for import without manual location cleanup.
monetization: one-time — physical counts are periodic and must work in basements, warehouses, and poor-connectivity environments.
constraints: Barcode camera access requires clear permission; local photo notes may expose stock/site data; CSV formats must be documented and untrusted imports safely parsed.
why_distinct: It is a controlled physical count pass and variance artifact, not a broad inventory/POS clone.
